newsitem.title: USA: New benefits found to alcohol, nicotine - study.
newsitem.headline: New benefits found to alcohol, nicotine - study.

text.p: Health hazards of drinking and smoking are well known but two studies released on Friday disclosed some medical benefits from alcohol and nicotine.

The studies, published separately in the March 1 issue of Annals of Internal Medicine, found that moderate alcohol consumption can decrease the risk of angina pectoris heart disease as well as heart attacks and that nicotine "patches" can help treat the intestinal ailment ulcerative colitis.
But the studies warned there were pitfalls to using either alcohol or nicotine in the search for better health.
"It is tricky," Dr. Frank Davidoff, editor of the medical journal said. "For both nicotine and alcohol there's obviously major downsides."
The alcohol study, conducted by researchers at the Brigham and Womens Hospital in Boston, followed 22,000 male doctors who were in good health when they enrolled in the study between 1981 and 1984.

It found those who had two or more drinks a day had a 56 percent lower risk of angina and a 44 percent lower risk of heart attack than men who had less than one drink per week. Similar but lesser benefits were noted among men who had one drink per day

Previous studies have documented a reduced risk of heart attacks among moderate drinkers but the Boston study is the first to show a reduced risk of angina, a less severe form of heart disease in which a diminished oxygen supply to the heart causes chest pains.

The study also found an increased cancer death rate among men who had two or more drinks per day. But overall, men who had between two and six drinks per week showed a lower total death rate, it said.

The study said any decision to increase alcohol consumption for health reasons should be made on a case-by-case basis. "The prospect of heavier drinking and its associated problems complicates any policy recommendation that lifelong abstainers begin drinking or that occasional drinkers increase their alcohol consumption," it said.
Instead, people should discuss the issue with their doctors before deciding whether an extra drink was worthwhile.

The nicotine study conducted by researchers at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota found that patients suffering from mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, which is an inflammation of the colon, experienced a reduction of symptoms when treated with strong doses of nicotine through skin patches.

In the study, 39 percent of the 31 patients who received nicotine showed clinical improvement, compared with only 9 percent of 33 patients in a placebo group. The treatments did not lead to a remission of the disease, the study said.
The study, prompted by findings that smokers were less likely to suffer from ulcerative colitis, also confirmed two previous studies of nicotine patches in treating the disease.

But it also found that 77 percent of the patients reported adverse reactions to the nicotine such as skin ailments, nausea and dizziness and 13 percent had to quit treatment because of the side effects.

While smokers have a lower rate of ulcerative colitis, it said, they have a higher rate of a similar intestinal ailment called Crohn's disease. It remained unclear what effect nicotine patches would have on Crohn's disease patients.
Davidoff said the results of the two studies further illustrated what has long been known to the medical profession but perhaps unrealized by the general public.

"People tend to think of certain kinds of drugs or chemicals as being either good or bad. But every single person that's ever studied pharmacology ... knows that every drug can be either therapeutic or toxic (depending on the dose)."
